extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of science; scientists and philosophers interested in foundations of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length treatment describing what counts as a scientific law, the conditions under which laws claim universality, and the epistemic limits of science (causation, probability, perception). Useful for evaluating scientific claims, methodology, and the boundary between science and metaphysics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final test of scientific law: comparison with facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The only final test we have of the truth of any law... is the actual comparison of the results of the formula with the facts themselves — that is, historical observation or physical experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws must be confronted with empirical observation/experiment; this empirical test distinguishes hypothesis from scientific law. The text notes that laws can be replaced by wider generalisations when new facts demand it. (Includes Herschel quote: 'The grand, and indeed only, character of truth is its capability of enduring the test of universal experience, and coming unchanged out of every possible form of fair discussion.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific laws are provisional and replaceable
rubrics_metrics.description: A product of a rational analysis of facts, [a law] is always liable to be replaced by a wider generalisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific progress routinely revises or replaces formulas; no formula should be treated as absolutely final. Historical examples and the idea that even long-standing formulas may be altered with advances in knowledge are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of scientific law is relative to the human mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The universality, the absolute character, which we attribute to scientific law is really relative to the human mind. It is conditioned by (1) the perceptive faculty and (2) the reflective faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of universality presuppose broadly similar perceptive and reflective faculties among 'normal' humans; this conditions applicability and must be recognized when asserting universal laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification requires resemblance in structure and action
rubrics_metrics.description: When we classify a number of things together and give them the same name, we can only mean to signify that they closely resemble each other in structure and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categories and terms should be used to group things that genuinely resemble one another in relevant respects; e.g., 'human beings' as a class presumes similarity in perceptive/reflective faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptive faculty is selective and shapes reality
rubrics_metrics.description: The perceptive faculty selects certain sense-impressions, and these form for it reality; objective reality does not consist of the same sense-impressions for man and dog.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that observers' sense-organs and perceptual selection shape the data available to science (dog vs man example); laws may reflect observer-dependent selection effects and evolutionary shaping of perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective faculty coordinates with perceptive faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: The perceptive and reflective faculties have been developed in co-ordination, so that the former accepts what, in wide limits, can be analysed by the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific formulation depends on a fit between what is perceived and what can be analysed; this coordination helps explain why perceptions can be expressed in brief formulae, but one must not assume analysis has already occurred merely because perceptions are structured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of scientific law may be conditioned by simplicity of senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Our sense-impressions are indeed complex in their grouping, but they come to us by very few and comparatively simple channels... The simplicity of the scientific law may therefore be partly conditioned by the simplicity of the modes in which sense-impressions are received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The concision of laws can reflect limits of sensory input and cognitive processing; this warns against overinterpreting simplicity as evidence of metaphysical simplicity in the world itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science must remain agnostic about the supersensuous
rubrics_metrics.description: We have no right to infer that order, mind, or reason — all human characters or human conceptions falling on this side of sense-impressions — exist on the other side of sense-impressions. Scientifically we must remain agnostic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims about realities beyond possible sensation (supersensuous) are not scientific; natural theology and metaphysics that assert knowledge of the supersensuous are treated as pseudo-science. Science should not project human concepts into the unknowable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid replacing ignorance with unwarranted hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: An honest confession of our ignorance and not mistrust in our fundamental principles — no meaningless hunt after unknown origins in the supersensuous, until the known field of perceptions has been shown incapable of yielding the needful basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When knowledge is incomplete (origins of life, higher faculties, weather historically), prefer admitting ignorance over positing speculative causes beyond the field of possible observation. Examples: origin of species, weather, Saturn's rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish nomic routine from scientific law/formula
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two distinct meanings to natural law: the mere routine of perception, and the scientific law or formula describing the field of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise about which sense of 'law' is intended; reason 'in' natural law arises only when we speak of the scientific/formula sense, and that reason is placed there by the human mind rather than inferred to exist beyond perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science as description of past and probabilistic belief about future
rubrics_metrics.description: Science for the past is a description, for the future a belief; it is not... an explanation if that means showing the necessity of any sequence. That it will continue to recur in the future is a matter of belief expressed in the concept probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific claims about future events are probabilistic, not certainties. Science cannot demonstrate inherent necessity; it assesses overwhelming probability based on past experience (example: improbability of a cosmic cataclysm tomorrow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics (and science) aims at simple description not metaphysical agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanics is the science of motion; its object is the complete description in the simplest possible manner of such motions as occur in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific disciplines aim to describe regularities simply rather than invoke 'dead' or 'living' metaphysical agents; avoid the popular misperception that science posits inherent agents in matter producing change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological conservatism: do not assume new causes unnecessarily
rubrics_metrics.description: Science — refusing to infer wildly where it cannot know, and unwilling to assume new causes where the old have not yet been shown insufficient — treats the 'dead matter' of the materialist as a world of sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explanations in terms of known causes until evidence forces the introduction of new ones; do not postulate extra-empirical causes prematurely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise terms and defined limits for 'knowledge' and 'explanation'
rubrics_metrics.description: Danger arises when we employ terms without concise meaning and clearly defined limits... The words explain and explanation are used in the sense of the descriptive how, and not the determinative why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define key terms (e.g., 'explain') carefully to avoid category errors; restrict 'explanation' to descriptive formulations when that is the intended usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mystery (impenetrable) from ignorance (subduable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science proclaims mystery where others profess knowledge. There is mystery enough in the universe of sensation and in its capacity... There is mystery enough here, only let us clearly distinguish it from ignorance within the field of possible knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some questions are permanently outside scientific reach (impenetrable mystery) while others are provisional unknowns to be addressed by further inquiry; do not conflate the two.
